report:
Contrary to your initial premise, robust scientific evidence shows that the answer is **yes**: offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) significantly increases overall HIV testing uptake.

Numerous randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic reviews consistently demonstrate that providing self-testing options alongside standard facility-based services leads more people to get tested:

1. **Doubled Uptake in General Populations:** A systematic review and meta-analysis published in *EClinicalMedicine* found that offering HIVST doubled the uptake of HIV testing in the general population compared to standard HIV testing services alone (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext).
2. **Increased Reach Among Key & High-Risk Groups:** A meta-analysis of RCTs among key populations found that distributing free HIV self-testing kits substantially increased testing uptake compared to standard of care across diverse delivery models (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z).
3. **Overcoming Barriers to Access:** Systematic reviews evaluating HIVST implementation in Africa and globally show that self-testing increases both first-time testing and overall testing frequency by overcoming key barriers such as stigma, inconvenience, long wait times, and privacy concerns (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0245498).
4. **Targeted Testing Frequency:** Evidence syntheses highlight that self-testing kits increase overall test frequency among underserved and high-risk groups who might otherwise avoid clinic-based testing (https://evidence.nihr.ac.uk/alert/self-testing-kits-increase-overall-hiv-testing-uptake-in-men-who-have-sex-with-men/).

Because HIV self-testing empowers individuals with a private, convenient option, global health authorities such as the World Health Organization strongly recommend HIVST to increase testing coverage.
